Stage 3 · Grammar

Three choices, and one of them is nothing

Most learners choose between a and the. The hard one is leaving it out.

Read these three sentences.
  • Life is competitive.
  • The school held sports days in a public park.
  • Everyone in the park could watch.
Why is it a park the first time and the park the second time?
Every English noun makes an article choice — including the choice to use none at all.

Articles are difficult for a specific reason: many languages either have none or use them on a different principle, so there is nothing to transfer. English uses them to answer a single question on your listener’s behalf — am I supposed to know which one you mean?

A or an introduces something new and countable: one of several, not yet identified. The school held sports days in a public park. The points at something both of you can identify — because it has already been mentioned, because there is only one, or because the situation makes it obvious. …so everyone in the park could watch. The shift from a to the between those two clauses is the system working exactly as designed.

The third option is no article at all, and this is the one that matters most in this lesson. Plural and uncountable nouns take no article when you are talking about things in general. Life is competitive. Children need exercise. Competition is healthy. Adding the to any of these narrows the claim to particular children or a particular competition, which is not what the speaker means. The life is competitive is the error this lesson exists to fix.

One safety net catches a large proportion of remaining mistakes: a singular countable noun can never stand alone. If you have written race, referee or decision in the singular, something must come in front of it — a, the, my, this. There is no correct sentence in which it stands bare.

Before you look at the table: the table below sorts the choices by the question your listener would ask. Read the middle column first; the examples will then look like consequences rather than exceptions.
The three choices

— (nothing)plural or uncountable, meaning things in generalChildren need exercise. · Life is competitive. · Sport teaches teamwork.
The fixed phrases — no article at all
TypeNo articleBut…

Ask whether the listener already knows which one. If yes, the. If not, a. If you do not mean a particular one at all — plural or uncountable, in general — leave it out.

General statements take no article. Not The life is competitive but Life is competitive. Not The children need exercise (unless you mean some particular children) but Children need exercise.

Places for their purpose lose the article. At school means studying. At the school means at that building, perhaps to fix the roof. The same split runs through hospital, bed, prison and church.

Superlatives always take the. The best team, the fastest runner — because there is only one, so both of you know which.

Full grammar reference — articles — a / an, the, and the zero article

What it is

Every English noun phrase makes an article choice, including the choice to use none. A / an introduces one of several, not yet identified. The points to a specific one that both speaker and listener can identify. The zero article — no article at all — is used with plural and uncountable nouns when you mean things in general.

What it means, and what it does

The article tells your listener whether they are supposed to know which one you mean. I saw a referee introduces someone new; I saw the referee assumes you know which. Beyond that, the zero article carries the whole idea of generality: Life is competitive and Children need exercise are statements about life and children as such, and adding the would turn them into statements about particular ones.

When and why we use it

Articles are difficult for a specific reason: many languages either have none or use them on a different principle, so there is nothing to transfer. English uses them to answer a single question on your listener’s behalf — am I supposed to know which one you mean?

A or an introduces something new and countable: one of several, not yet identified. The school held sports days in a public park. The points at something both of you can identify — because it has already been mentioned, because there is only one, or because the situation makes it obvious. …so everyone in the park could watch. The shift from a to the between those two clauses is the system working exactly as designed.

The third option is no article at all, and this is the one that matters most in this lesson. Plural and uncountable nouns take no article when you are talking about things in general. Life is competitive. Children need exercise. Competition is healthy. Adding the to any of these narrows the claim to particular children or a particular competition, which is not what the speaker means. The life is competitive is the error this lesson exists to fix.

One safety net catches a large proportion of remaining mistakes: a singular countable noun can never stand alone. If you have written race, referee or decision in the singular, something must come in front of it — a, the, my, this. There is no correct sentence in which it stands bare.

Typical situations

Articles are unavoidable — every noun you write requires a decision. They matter most in general statements, in definitions, in academic and argued writing, and in the fixed expressions listed below.

  • First mention of something countable — a / an — one of many, new to the listener.The school held sports days in a public park.
  • Second mention, or already identified — the — we both know which.Everyone in the park could watch.
  • Only one of its kind — the — the listener can identify it without being told.The government has announced new plans.
  • Superlatives and ordinals — the — there is only one.The best team doesn’t always win. The first race is at ten.
  • Things in general — zero article with plurals and uncountables.— Children need exercise. — Competition is healthy.
  • Jobs and roles — a / an after be or become.She’s a referee in the district league.
  • Places used for their purpose — zero article.That’s what I learnt at — school. He’s in — hospital.
  • Fixed expressions — learnt whole.in — general · by — bus · take — part · on the other hand

How it differs from similar structures

at school = studying · at the school = at that building, perhaps to fix the roof. The same split runs through hospital, prison, church, bed.
Children need exercise = children in general · The children need exercise = these particular children. The article changes the scope of the claim.

How to build it

a / an + singular countable noun  (first mention, one of many)
the + any noun  (both of us know which one)
— (nothing) + plural or uncountable noun  (things in general)
the + superlative / ordinal / unique thing
a or an?By sound, not spelling: a university /j-/, an hour /aʊ-/, a European, an MP /em/.
Singular countablealways needs an article or another determiner: a race, the race, my race — never bare race.
Plural countable— races (in general) · the races (those particular ones)
Uncountable— competition (in general) · the competition we entered
Superlativethe fastest runner, the most competitive school
JobsShe is a teacher. — not She is teacher.
Places for purposeat — school, in — hospital, to — bed, at — home, to — work
Same places as buildingsat the school my son goes to · at the hospital where she works

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • the is pronounced /ðə/ before a consonant sound and /ði/ before a vowel sound: the team vs the athlete.
  • A stressed /ðiː/ signals uniqueness or emphasis: He’s THE best player in the league.
  • a is normally reduced to /ə/ and is almost inaudible, which is why learners often do not hear it and then omit it in writing.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • A singular countable noun can never stand alone. If you have race, referee, decision in the singular, you must put something in front: a, the, my, this. This one rule fixes a large share of article errors.
  • General statements take the zero article: Life is competitive, not The life is competitive. This is the error the whole lesson exists to fix.
  • The is used before superlatives, ordinals, and things there is only one of (the sun, the government, the internet).
  • Country names normally take no article (Kazakhstan, Britain), but plurals and names containing a common noun do (the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the Czech Republic).
  • Meals, transport and general ideas take no article: have — lunch, by — car, in — general. But: the lunch we had yesterday, the bus to Almaty.
  • Many languages either have no articles or use them differently. Do not translate; test each noun with the questions in the tip below.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • The life is competitive. → Life is competitive.A general idea takes no article.
  • She is referee in the district league. → She is a referee in the district league.A singular countable noun needs an article.
  • He is fastest runner in the school. → He is the fastest runner in the school.Superlatives take the.
  • I learnt that when I was at the school. → I learnt that when I was at school.At school = while studying.
  • The competition is healthy, but taking part matters more. → Competition is healthy, but taking part matters more.A general idea takes no article.
  • We went there by the bus. → We went there by bus.Transport takes no article in this phrase.

More examples in context

  • first mentionThe school used to hold sports days in a public park.
  • second mention…so everyone in the park could watch.
  • uniqueThe government has announced that tournaments are to be re-introduced.
  • superlativeIt is the most competitive event in the school year.
  • general, plural— Children need exercise more than they need medals.
  • general, uncountable— Competition is healthy, but taking part is more important.
  • jobShe has been a referee for eight years.
  • place for purposeThat’s what I learnt when I was at — school.
  • place as buildingWe met at the school where she teaches.
  • fixed phrase— In general, non-competitive activities suit younger children better.

A tip for remembering it

Run three questions in order for every noun. 1 Do I mean things in general, plural or uncountable? → no article. 2 Does my listener already know which one? → the. 3 Otherwise, if it is singular and countable → a / an. And remember the safety net: a lone singular countable noun is always an error.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. A / an = one of many, first mention; the = the one we both know; no article = things in general.
  2. A singular countable noun always needs an article or another determiner.
  3. General statements with plurals and uncountables take no article.
  4. Superlatives, ordinals and unique things take the.
  5. A or an is chosen by sound, not spelling.
  6. Places used for their purpose (at school, in hospital, to bed) take no article.
